The full published FY2028 street dispersion on AI-server revenue, a spread more than twice Dell's entire FY2026 AI revenue, is the fourth-largest swing in terminal operating income and the second-smallest in cumulative cash. Working capital moves no operating income at all and $8.1B of cumulative cash between its bounds, and it is invisible in a profit-and-loss-only model, which is what the street publishes.

17.5 Where the base case departs from consensus

FY2027 FY2028 FY2029 FY2030 FY2031
Model base revenue 167,411 182,537 184,248 180,389 177,464
Consensus revenue 170,982 198,204 220,592 235,734 236,428
Difference (2.1)% (7.9)% (16.5)% (23.5)% (24.9)%
Model base non-GAAP EPS 17.75 20.06 20.37 20.60 21.41
Consensus non-GAAP EPS 18.35 22.41 26.03 31.76 37.57
Difference (3.3)% (10.5)% (21.7)% (35.1)% (43.0)%

Consensus contributor counts decline from 26 at FY2028 to 15 at FY2029 to 3 at FY2030 and 2 at FY2031, so the outer-year comparison is against a very thin number. Consensus has revenue rising every year through FY2031 and therefore models no give-back of the roughly $18B of the FY2027 increment that comes from the price-levered lines. Consensus needs an operating-expense ratio of 7.63% by FY2029 and 5.50% by FY2031 against the 8.4% Q1 FY2027 print the CFO called the lowest in over 20 years, which is entirely a denominator effect. And gross margin runs the other way: the model's FY2030 rate of 17.9% is above the 17.2% consensus, because deflating pass-through dollars out of revenue lifts the rate even as gross profit dollars stay flat.

Bull-case flag. The bull case implies incremental operating margins of 12.6%, 14.1%, 16.6%, 17.9%, 17.7% and 17.4% across FY2027–FY2032. Dell's realized best consolidated incremental operating margin is 12.2%, with 11.6% in FY2025 and 10.6% in FY2026. Every bull year exceeds the historical best and four of six exceed it by more than four points. The bull's 12.6% non-GAAP operating margin on a 17%–19% gross margin also has no technology precedent: of 39 company-years in the reference class combining a 12%–22% gross margin with a 9%-plus operating margin above $20B of revenue, all 39 belong to Chevron, Exxon, Marathon, Boeing, Berkshire or Tesla. Base-case incremental operating margins of 10.3% in FY2027 and 8.5% in FY2028 are inside the realized record.

17.6 What the model inherits and cannot resolve

The model uses the $51,300M AI backlog figure, the CFO's and the only one that closes the roll-forward, against the $53,100M cited five days later. It anchors on the 10-K's $24,683M of FY2026 AI revenue against the $25.2B "shipped." It treats the AI backlog as a management series and cross-checks it against filed RPO, which covers roughly 63% of the balance of the FY2027 guide. It follows the 10-Q on the Q1 FY2027 CSG margin bridge, which the filing attributes to gross margin. And it takes FY2026 as year zero, so the unexplained $200M upward restatement of FY2024 CSG operating income does not propagate, though any comparison against "the FY2024 peak" inherits a restated number.

The model cannot settle six things.

  • What fraction of the $51,300M AI backlog is non-cancelable, which decides whether the FY2027–FY2028 AI line is a contract or a pipeline.
  • The Dell-IP versus third-party split of the storage line in dollars, which drives the core gross margin the whole ISG structure depends on.
  • How much of the FY2027 traditional-server and CSG price increase reverses, and on what lag, which management names three causes for and quantifies none of.
  • How much FY2027 demand is pull-forward, which Michael Dell conceded exists without sizing.
  • Who the 12%-of-revenue customer is, and what the combined trade, financing and inventory exposure to it amounts to, since a single-counterparty cancellation cannot be represented in a driver model built on aggregate orders.
  • What repurchase price is assumed, since the model reports buyback dollars and share count separately because linking them requires a price, and consensus has the same gap.

18. Risks

A gap at the top of this section. Trade policy, tariffs and export controls are not covered below. The FY2026 10-K names tariffs five times and export controls twice without sizing either. Non-US revenue was 45% of the FY2026 total, manufacturing is in China, Malaysia, Brazil, India, Poland and Ireland, and the AI product is export-controlled NVIDIA silicon. That exposure runs through both the sovereign-AI demand leg and the cost-of-goods line.

R1 — Fixed-volume, floating-price component commitments into a memory cycle that has already run 5x (severe)

Mechanism. Dell buys memory it has committed to take at prices set after the fact and resells it inside servers and PCs whose prices it resets roughly continuously. That works while memory inflates and reverses when prices turn: the committed volume arrives at a cost struck near the top, the finished inventory is recorded on the balance sheet at that cost, and the selling price declines because the whole industry's prices decline together. The 10-K states that inventory is at the lower of cost or net realizable value and that less favourable demand or market conditions may require additional write-downs.

Exposure. Inventories rose 124% and production materials 140% over five quarters, to $15,052M and $10,634M. Purchase obligations went from $18.8B to $20.8B, and the beyond-twelve-month tranche nearly doubled from $2.0B to $3.9B in a single quarter, which is the multi-year supplier lock-in Clarke described. The strategic-supplier exclusion on top of both is unquantified. A 10% write-down of production materials alone would be roughly $1.1B, about 13% of FY2026 GAAP operating income [estimate]. The revenue-side exposure is larger than the margin-side exposure: roughly $18B of the $53.5B FY2027 revenue increment and roughly $17B of the $27B guidance raise are in lines management attributes substantially to price and content.

Leading indicators. Server DRAM contract price direction; the production-materials line in the Q2 FY2027 10-Q; the beyond-twelve-month purchase-obligation tranche; whether the strategic-supplier exclusion language survives or gets quantified; any inventory-related charge in cost of net revenue.

R2 — AI revenue is roughly a quarter as profitable per dollar as the rest of ISG, and the mix keeps climbing (severe)

Mechanism and exposure. At management's stated mid-single-digit rate, $10B of AI revenue produces roughly $1.24B less operating income than $10B of non-AI ISG revenue.▪ Applied to the backlog, $51.3B converts to roughly $2.6B of operating income at the target rate against roughly $8.9B at the rest-of-ISG rate. AI mix went from 21.7% of consolidated revenue in FY2026 to 36.8% in Q1 FY2027, and the FY2027 guide keeps it near 36%. At a 5% operating margin, 100 basis points on $60B of FY2027 AI revenue is $600M, about 4.7% of the operating income the guide implies. The FY2026 10-K reworded the AI risk factor to say large orders can affect "our gross margins and results of operations," adding the word gross, and Q1 FY2027 delivered exactly that.

Leading indicators. ISG operating margin against the guided sequential improvement in Q2 FY2027; AI mix as a share of ISG; any softening of the mid-single-digit language; operating expense as a percentage of revenue, since that offset is nearly exhausted.

R3 — Receivables growing faster than revenue while the reserve rate halved and customer concentration appeared (high)

Mechanism and exposure. Accounts receivable went $10,300M to $17,585M to $25,854M across fifteen months, up 151% against 88% revenue growth in the latest quarter. The allowance held at $77M and the reserve rate declined from 0.61% a year earlier to 0.30%. Reverting to that year-earlier rate would require an $81M incremental charge [estimate], which is small against $3,438M of quarterly net income. Concentration arrived at the same time: one customer at 12% of FY2026 consolidated revenue, roughly $13.6B, with substantially all of it in ISG. The counterparty class matters because neocloud balance sheets are themselves levered against GPU collateral, with CoreWeave's total obligations reported at $24.9B by mid-2026 against under $8B in 2024 [web].

Leading indicators. The allowance-to-receivables ratio in the Q2 FY2027 10-Q; days sales outstanding; whether a 10% customer reappears in the FY2027 concentration note and at what share; the volume of receivables sold without recourse moving from immaterial to disclosed.

R4 — DFS is scaling into a weaker credit mix while being used to pull demand forward (high)

Mechanism and exposure. Originations grew 42% to $11.9B in FY2026 and the 10-K attributes the increase in financing receivables primarily to AI-optimized servers. The Higher-grade share of gross customer receivables declined from 54.7% to 45.1% in one year. Of the $7,901M originated in FY2026, 33.8% is graded Higher and 14.6% Lower, against 43.3% and 10.4% for the FY2025 vintage. Losses have not moved — the principal charge-off rate was 0.5%, 0.6%, 0.2% and 0.3% in Q1 FY2027 — because the risk is forward and seasoning-dependent. Separately, adjusted free cash flow, the base for the 80%-plus return commitment, adds back the funding of financing receivables, $2,740M in FY2026 against $951M in FY2025.

Leading indicators. The credit-grade vintage table in the FY2027 10-K; the charge-off rate; originations growth against revenue growth; whether the 7:1 DFS allocation ratio is changed.

R5 — The growth is funded by payables, and the working-capital swing reverses if the order book stalls (high)

Mechanism and exposure. Q1 FY2027 operating cash flow of $4,081M contained an $11,661M payables inflow against an $8,331M receivable build and a $4,715M inventory build. Excluding the payables movement, operating cash flow for the quarter was negative $7,580M. Current assets of $70,607M against current liabilities of $74,598M give a 0.95x current ratio. Days payable is stable at roughly 114 days, so the payables growth tracks scale; a 10-day contraction at the Q1 run rate is roughly a $4.0B outflow. Super Micro, running the same model at smaller scale, produced negative operating cash flow of $6.8B for its FY2026 as inventory and receivables rose sharply [web]; Dell has avoided that only because its payables base is large enough to fund the build.

Leading indicators. Accounts payable divided by cost of net revenue; operating cash flow excluding the payables movement; the appearance of supplier prepayments or deposits, of which none are disclosed; the current ratio.

R6 — Pull-forward and price-induced demand destruction, both already acknowledged (high)

Mechanism and exposure. Customers buying ahead of price increases borrow from future periods, and price increases past a threshold destroy demand outright. Management confirmed both in the same call. The FY2027 guide implies the second half at roughly 48% of full-year revenue against a historical 51.3%, and management attributes the shape entirely to supply. That attribution is untestable from outside, because a supply-constrained second half and a pulled-forward first half produce the same reported numbers. CSG operating margin is guided from 8.0% down to roughly 6% in one quarter.

Leading indicators. The Q2 FY2027 CSG operating margin against the roughly 6% guide; the commercial CSG demand streak, at nine consecutive quarters; whether traditional-server unit growth persists or reverts to the FY2026 pattern of price-only growth.

R7 — Backlog and orders are unaudited, undefined and not reconcilable to the filed measure (medium-high)

Dell's AI backlog figure is disclosed only on earnings calls. Filed RPO was $82B and $97B at the two most recent dates, with 78% and 80% expected within twelve months. RPO excludes amounts owed under cancelable contracts where there is no substantive termination penalty, and includes product backlog only where Dell determines the manufacturing orders are non-cancelable. How much of the $51.3B AI backlog clears that test is not disclosed. The two series do not move together: AI backlog rose $8.3B between the two dates while RPO rose $15B, and twelve-month RPO of $78B covers about half the FY2027 revenue guide. Two contradictions remain unresolved: $51.3B versus $53.1B five days apart, and $24,683M of recognized revenue against $25.2B "shipped." Leading indicator: whether Dell ever publishes a backlog-to-RPO bridge.

R8 — Single-vendor roadmap dependence and the Vera Rubin transition (medium)

Every named AI platform is NVIDIA's. Second-half FY2027 revenue depends on a generational transition management expects to ship in that window, and backlog composition at Q4 FY2026 was described as predominantly Grace Blackwell with no Vera Rubin in the pipeline. The FY2027 guide loads $60B of AI revenue with $15.5B guided in Q2 and the balance weighted to a half-year that depends on a platform not yet in volume; a one-quarter slip moves roughly $15B of revenue across the fiscal-year boundary. Leading indicators: NVIDIA's own Rubin schedule; Dell's Q2 FY2027 AI-server revenue against the $15.5B guide.

R9 — Governance and capital-structure asymmetries (medium, structural)

Michael Dell and the Silver Lake stockholders held approximately 91.7% of voting power on 53.8% of economic ownership as of 2026-03-09, and only Class C trades. Key-person dependence on Michael Dell is a named risk factor and he is also the controlling stockholder, so succession and control are the same risk. The July 2026 Texas redomestication installed a 3% derivative-suit threshold and a charter jury-trial waiver on internal entity claims, and the board flagged that a body of case law interpreting the Texas amendments has not yet developed. Silver Lake's holding has declined 68% since 2019 and it was still selling into the advance in July 2026 at an average near $440. A new risk factor appeared in FY2026 stating that the amount and frequency of share repurchases may fluctuate, filed in the same year the authorization was raised $10B and repurchases doubled.

R10 — Cybersecurity, escalated in the FY2026 text and never sized (medium)

Dell states plainly that it has already been breached by attacks leveraging compromised credentials of partners, vendors, employees and customers. The FY2026 edition added vendors to that list, extended the consequence to third parties' operations, added contractual liability to the loss categories, and named generative and agentic AI on both sides of the attack surface. The board moved from annual to bi-annual cyber reviews. The leading indicator here is an 8-K.

R11 — Second-order and named but small (low, tracked)

An ERISA class action over 401(k) plan investment selection was filed 2026-01-28 in the Western District of Texas with damages unspecified. Goodwill and intangibles of $24.1B are 24% of total assets with no impairment disclosed; the denominator is growing faster than the numerator, which reduces the ratio without reducing the absolute exposure. Government business is named as a significant source and never sized. Tax audit language was escalated in FY2026 from a substantial increase in tax expense to a material impact on results, financial position and cash flows.

Correlation: the bad quarter is one event

Nine of these risks are the same cycle seen from different sides, and they arrive in sequence. Server DRAM contract prices flatten and then decline, and the deceleration from +90%–95% quarter over quarter in 1Q CY2026 to an expected +13%–18% in 3Q CY2026 is already the first step. Dell takes fixed-volume deliveries at prices struck near the top and the lower-of-cost-or-net-realizable-value test applies to $15.1B of inventory. The price component of traditional-server and CSG revenue reverses, which is roughly $18B of the FY2027 increment. Customers who bought ahead stop buying. Orders slow, so accounts payable stops growing and the $11,661M inflow that funded the quarter's receivable and inventory build disappears. AI backlog conversion slows into the Vera Rubin transition, so the segment that was supposed to absorb the fixed cost base arrives late at a 5% operating margin. Receivables of $25.9B reserved at 0.30% and DFS receivables of $14.0B written to a mix 9.6 points worse than a year ago season into a slower environment. And buybacks sized off a measure that adds back DFS funding become harder to maintain, which is why the repurchase-variability risk factor was added in FY2026. Steps one, two, four in part, and five are already observable in the reported numbers.

19. Source disclosure

Local databases used. The research archive supplied ten 10-Ks covering FY2017–FY2026, thirteen 10-Qs covering Q1 FY2023 through Q1 FY2027, 39 earnings-call transcripts from Q3 FY2017 through Q1 FY2027 unbroken, 60 presentation transcripts including all ten Securities Analyst Meetings and Shareholder-Analyst Calls, and ten investor decks with 458 rendered slides. SEC XBRL company facts under CIK 0001571996 supplied the consolidated three statements. Peer and value-chain filings were read directly from the archive for NVIDIA, HPE, Super Micro, NetApp, Micron, SanDisk, Western Digital, HP Inc., Apple, Arista, IBM and Meta. The Proxy project supplied eight parsed DEF 14A filings from 2018 to 2025. A live Bloomberg terminal supplied all prices, consensus estimates, the base-rate universe of 518 index members and 14,337 company-years, the 62-name hand-built reference class, and the 24-row public comparable table.

Sources added to the archive. Seven additional 10-Qs were archived, taking the quarterly set from six to thirteen filings, which is what makes the twelve-quarter segment series possible. The FY2026 DEF 14A filed 2026-05-15 was pulled from EDGAR because it was not in the Proxy store, along with six 8-Ks. Peer filings for HPE, Super Micro, NetApp and Arista were added to the archive.

Gaps and failures.

  • Daloopa is not among the sources, so the reconciliation ran as filings and XBRL against Bloomberg only. One discrepancy is therefore unarbitrated: Bloomberg's EBITDA runs $239M–$766M, or 2%–4%, above operating income plus cash-flow depreciation and amortization in every year from FY2020 to FY2026, with the gap stable at roughly $240–340M from FY2021.
  • No sell-side digest coverage exists for DELL, zero rows across 39 reports. Every qualitative sell-side view is web-sourced and tagged. There is no local record of how the street narrated the 2024 AI-margin de-rating or the 2026 re-rating.
  • No 10K-redlines coverage exists for DELL, so year-over-year textual work was done directly off the archived 10-K text with a line-level diff on Item 1A for FY2023–FY2026 plus first-appearance searches across all ten years. Nine years of drift in Item 1, Item 7 and the competition language were not diffed.
  • IDC's own pages return HTTP 403 to both direct fetch and Firecrawl. Every unit and share figure comes from trade-press summaries with prior-year vendor columns back-solved from disclosed growth rates. Dell'Oro data-center switching data was never obtained, so Dell's networking line is never sized.
  • The Call-extraction guidance scorecard for DELL is unusable because the company directory was scaffolded with a December fiscal year end, so every quarter identifier is one fiscal year off and resolves silently to the wrong year's call. Every guidance and actual figure was rebuilt from the fiscal-correct archive instead.
  • CoreWeave, TSMC, Seagate, Lenovo and Pure Storage were not archived, so the customer-side economics in Section 5 and the foundry and hard-drive layers of the dollar decomposition depend on secondary reporting.
  • No expert-network or primary-channel source was consulted.
  • Pre-FY2017 history is unavailable under the current registrant, which has exactly ten 10-Ks on EDGAR. Earlier history is filed under Dell Inc., CIK 0000826083, and EMC Corp, CIK 0000790070, and was not pulled. The EMC transaction is therefore graded on newsroom copies of press releases with no S-4, no merger proxy and no unaffected-price premium, and Dell's own 1990s growth record is absent from the base rates.
  • The price record covers 7.6 years, because Class C began regular-way trading on 2018-12-28 and the Class V tracking stock is not chained to it.
  • Ten weeks before 2026-08-12 have no company source. The latest 10-Q is dated 2026-06-09 and the latest transcript 2026-06-02, and the archive holds no 8-K of any type in that window. EDGAR filings between those dates and 2026-08-12 are not covered.
  • Bloomberg publishes no cash-flow consensus for DELL and no segment- or product-level consensus, so every segment-level street expectation in Section 14 is a residual build.

Web sources. Roughly 40 distinct pages across about 25 domains are cited. The heaviest use is trade-press summaries of IDC and TrendForce releases (idc.com, trendforce.com, electronicsweekly.com, biztechreports.com, infotechlead.com, networkworld.com, thetechoutlook.com, blocksandfiles.com, techspot.com, tomshardware.com), company press releases (gartner.com, netapp.com, lenovo.com, acer.com, dell.com, sophos.com, prnewswire.com), and financial press (fortune.com, reuters via finance.yahoo.com, cnbc.com, qz.com, 247wallst.com, tikr.com, investing.com, stockanalysis.com). Every web-sourced claim is tagged inline and the material ones are excerpted in Appendix B.

Claims flagged as [web, unverified]. One claim is flagged: the S&P Global rating action titled as an upgrade of Dell to BBB+, published around June 2026, whose page returns HTTP 403. The Fitch upgrade to BBB+ on 2025-09-30 is verified. Moody's current rating was not located.

Estimates by method. Thirty [estimate: ...] tags appear in the body, covering fourteen distinct estimated quantities, each with its bounds. By method:

  • Five are simultaneous solves or residual decompositions on disclosed segment expense categories: the AI and core ISG gross margins, the AI-versus-non-AI operating income split, the CSG device-and-attach split, and the storage array residual.
  • Four are third-party-share-times-market-size derivations with prior years back-solved: the CY1Q25 server vendor column, the branded server pool, external storage shares, and PC unit counts.
  • Two are unit-count builds from external trackers: AI rack-equivalents and traditional-server units.
  • One is a bottom-up addressable-market build from participants' filings.
  • One is a payback calculation on external rack prices and rental rates.
  • One is an allocation-based return on capital for CSG.

Internal figure conflicts left unresolved. The following figures differ between sections and are not reconciled.

  • Three closing prices for 2026-08-12. $464.05 in the front-matter capitalization table and throughout §15, $463.08 in the §10 ownership and option arithmetic, and $463.19 in the §16 comparable table. Each section is internally consistent at its own price; the multiples, market capitalization and enterprise value used everywhere else are on $464.05.
  • Market capitalization against share count. $299,539M at $464.05 implies about 645.5M shares, against the 649M shares outstanding at 2026-05-01 shown two rows above it. The difference is consistent with repurchases between 2026-05-01 and the pull date, but the document does not state a current count.
  • Total debt at 2026-05-01. The front-matter note gives $31,906M against §12's carrying value of $31,161M and principal of $31,413M. The $745M difference is consistent with the operating-lease liability being included in the enterprise-value build, which is how §15.1 constructs enterprise value in every prior year, but the label says GAAP total debt.
  • FY2020 and FY2021 revenue. §13.1 shows $84,815M and $86,670M on a continuing-operations basis; §10.4's uses-of-cash table shows $92,154M and $94,224M as reported with VMware consolidated. Growth rates and multi-year compound rates differ accordingly, and §13.1's FY2020 revenue decline of 6% is measured against an FY2019 figure that still includes VMware.
  • FY2021 GAAP diluted EPS. $4.22 in §13.1, total including discontinued operations; $2.93 in §15.1, continuing operations, which the 24.9x trailing multiple in that table is computed on. §15.1 uses the total figure for FY2020 and the continuing figure for FY2021.
  • FY2023 share repurchases. $2,800M in §12's dilution table, $2,883M in §10.4's uses-of-cash and capital-returned tables, and $3,272M in §13.1's cash-flow row. The $2,883M figure is the one the $18,335M cumulative return and the $15,856M programme-to-date figure are built from.
  • FY2017 operating cash flow. $2,222M in §10.4 against $2,367M in §13.1. The ten-year total of $75,008M uses $2,222M. Every other year matches across the two tables.
  • FY2018 ISG revenue. $30,917M in §9's EMC inflection against $30,652M in §11's eight-year ex-AI growth calculation. §1.3's 1.5% FY2018–FY2024 compound rate is consistent with $30,917M; §11's 2.08% rate is computed off $30,652M.
  • Dell's CY2025 PC unit share and market growth. §1.3 uses Gartner, 15.3% share on a market up 9.1%, with 41.4M units in §1.2. §4.3 and §13.4 use IDC, 14.4% share on a market up 8.1%, with about 41.0M units. Every share series in §4, §6, §8 and §13 is on the IDC basis; only §1.3 is on Gartner's.
  • The FY2027 guidance-raise table in §5. The four disclosed lines sum to a $26.3B raise against the $26.8B total stated in the same row, and the share-of-raise column sums to 98% against a stated 100%. The residual is consistent with a Corporate-and-other line that is not shown, which is also what the "within $200M of the stated midpoints" claim requires, and neither can be checked on the rows printed.
  • The storage non-array drag in §4.2. The reconciliation table shows the residual declining $489M on a $3,996M prior-year base, about twelve points of drag on the quarter's reported growth. The prose beneath it says about eight points, and §4.2, §6 and §8 all use six to nine points for the annual effect once the crossover ends.
  • The FY2026 working-capital bridge in §13.3. The four named cash-flow movements — receivables $7,022M, financing receivables $2,740M and inventories $3,987M against payables of $12,665M — net to a $1,084M use against the $871M source stated in the same sentence. The gap is other working-capital lines that are not named.
  • The cash conversion cycle at 2026-01-30. About −31 days in §1.4, computed on quarterly revenue and derived cost of net revenue against period-end balances, against −37 days in §13.3 on annual figures. Dell publishes neither.
  • Services as a share of Q1 FY2027 revenue. 12.9% in §1.2 against 13.1% in §5. Services revenue for the quarter is not disclosed in either place; both are derived.
  • The dividend arithmetic in §17.3. Compounding the modelled FY2028 dividend of $2.77 at the stated realized rate of 17.5% a year gives roughly $5.28 by FY2032 against the $6.02 stated in the same cell. The modelled $4.06 is exactly $2.77 grown at 10% a year.
  • Super Micro's period basis. §4.1 uses FY2025 revenue of $21,972M and the January–March 2026 quarter; §3.1 uses FY2026 revenue of $39,063M and the April–June 2026 quarter. The §4.1 line margins and two-year compound rate are computed off the older year.
  • The GB300 rack price used in §5's payback table. The $6.0–6.5M range is attributed to DigiTimes via Tom's Hardware, but the excerpt captured for that source in Appendix B reports Vera Rubin pricing to $8.8M and the 90% compute-tray share, and the other captured source reports $3M–$4M for GB300. Appendix B does not corroborate the $6.0–6.5M range, and the 2.8-year and 5.1-year payback rows use its midpoint.

20. What we still don't know, and what would resolve it

Material gaps

  1. How much memory Dell can secure for FY2027 is unknown. Management says FY2027 revenue is set by what Dell can source, and the volumes behind the $20.8B of purchase obligations are not disclosed. Resolution: a supply-coverage ratio bridging purchase obligations to the revenue guide, using disclosed obligations, Micron's bit-growth disclosure and published memory content per rack.
  2. Dell's tariff and export-control exposure is unquantified. The FY2026 10-K names tariffs five times and export controls twice without sizing either. Resolution: a sized exposure by manufacturing location and by export-controlled product line, against the 45% of revenue that is non-US.
  3. How Dell's AI revenue splits by region is not disclosed. Note 18 gives revenue by region, and Item 1 states that roughly 65% of ISG and roughly 60% of CSG revenue is Americas. The AI ramp is Americas-concentrated while the case for broadening beyond the neoclouds is sovereign AI, and the two cannot be reconciled on what Dell publishes.
  4. What drove the services decline is unknown. Services was 45.6% of FY2026 consolidated gross profit at a 44.8% margin and declined from $24,147M to $23,133M. The split of that decline between the Corporate-and-other runoff and core support attach is not disclosed, and the services attach rate on an AI rack is unknown. Nearly half of gross profit is undecomposed.
  5. The economics of Dell Financial Services are unquantified. Its financing revenue, its net spread over securitization cost, and its return on the $14.3B receivable book plus $2.5B of equipment under operating leases are all unknown, and residual value, which the 10-K discusses four times, is unsized.
  6. The premium Dell paid for EMC over an unaffected price is unknown. The S-4 and the merger proxy are filed under the pre-2017 registrants, Dell Inc. and EMC Corp.
  7. Dell's FY2017–FY2021 results are not comparable to FY2022 onward. Those years consolidate VMware and no pro-forma ex-VMware series exists, so every ten-year growth, margin, return and cash-conversion series spans a comparability break.
  8. The most recent Dell disclosure is dated 2026-06-09. Q2 FY2027 prints roughly two weeks after 2026-08-12, into a memory market that moved 90%–95% quarter over quarter and after a guide that moved $27B in one quarter.
  9. Every unit, price and market-share figure for Dell is second-hand, because IDC's own pages return HTTP 403 and Dell'Oro data is unavailable.
  10. The memory price path is not available as a dated series. It appears only as scattered quotes, so the FY2027 price assumptions cannot be tested against a market series.
  11. CoreWeave's capital-expenditure guide, backlog, GPU life and net loss are known only from secondary reporting. CoreWeave is the only AI customer Dell has ever named.

Questions that would change the analysis if answered

  • What fraction of the $51.3B AI backlog is non-cancelable? RPO includes manufacturing orders only where Dell judges them non-cancelable, and Dell has never said how much of the AI backlog meets that test. That number decides whether the FY2027–FY2028 AI line is a contract or a pipeline.
  • What is the Dell-IP versus third-party split of the $16,631M storage line, in dollars? It drives the roughly 40% core gross margin the entire ISG margin structure depends on, and it is the largest cumulative-cash driver in the model.
  • What is the AI-server gross margin, as distinct from the mid-single-digit operating income rate? Without it, the value Dell's integration adds over a bare NVIDIA rack cannot be isolated, and the whole dollar decomposition in Section 5 moves with it.
  • What operating expense does Dell allocate to the AI-server line internally? The reconciliation implies roughly 3% of AI revenue against 15.5% for the rest of ISG. If that is right, the AI business consumes almost none of the field sales, service and support infrastructure management describes as its advantage.
  • Who is the 12%-of-revenue customer, and what is the total exposure across trade receivables, financing receivables and inventory built against its orders?
  • How much of the traditional-server and CSG price increase reverses when memory normalizes, and on what lag? Management names component-cost pass-through, richer configurations and price realization, and quantifies none of the three.
  • How much of FY2027 demand is pull-forward? Michael Dell conceded "I'm sure there's some pull-forward, but we don't know how much" and no sizing has been offered.
  • What share of AI-server revenue is neocloud versus sovereign versus enterprise? Dell discloses customer count and never revenue mix, so the durability of the largest driver cannot be assessed and the unnamed 12% customer cannot be placed.
  • Will the FY2030 framework be re-based, and if not, is management implying flat-to-declining revenue from FY2028? The FY2027 guide already exceeds both FY2030 targets on management's own baseline.
  • What are the market-capitalization and adjusted-free-cash-flow thresholds on the COO's 2.5-million-share option? Without them, whether the roughly $803M of current intrinsic value is already effectively earned is unknown.
  • Why has recurring revenue not been quantified for ten quarters when it remains a defined term in both Item 1 and Item 7?
  • What is Dell's share of the AI-server market and which way is it moving? IDC publishes no vendor split inside accelerated servers, so the comparison in Section 4 is a point-in-time revenue comparison on mismatched periods with no share series behind it.
  • Where is the rack-integration capacity ceiling? Management says "we have the capacity — there's no capacity issue. It's parts, supply," and capital expenditure is 2.2% of revenue. Dell's integration throughput per quarter is not disclosed, so a shift in the constraint from parts to integration would not be visible in the current record.

Appendix A — Investor-presentation insights and key slides

Ten decks with 458 rendered slides span 2021 to 2026, including all three Securities Analyst Meetings in the window. Roughly 45% of the slide count is non-GAAP reconciliation appendices, balance-sheet reprints and guidance tables that duplicate the 8-K and 10-Q. What the decks add beyond the filings and transcripts:

  • A nine-year ISG P&L and a seven-year CSG P&L with operating margin on the face of the slide. The 10-K discloses segment operating income for three years. ISG operating margin never exceeded 13.2% in nine years and averaged about 11.8%, so FY2026's 11.7% is close to the segment's own decade norm. Informs §3 and §13.
  • The FY2026 estimated operating-margin cell is left blank on both segment slides while every historical year is filled in. ISG's $55.3B of revenue on $6.2B of operating income implies 11.2% and CSG's $50.0B on $3.2B implies 6.4%. Reported outcomes were 11.7% and 5.6%, so both segment guides were wrong within one quarter in opposite directions. Informs §8 and §10.
  • The three long-term frameworks side by side, with the segment splits behind them. Revenue 3%–4%, then 3%–4%, then 7%–9%; EPS 6%+, then 8%+, then 15%+; free-cash-flow return 40%–60%, then 80%+, then 80%+. ISG's target was raised twice, from 3%–5% to 11%–14%, tracking the AI ramp after the fact. CSG's has been 2%–3% at all three meetings against a realized −4.6% from FY2022 to FY2026, with the same three rationale bullets each time. Informs §8, §10 and §14.
  • A full eight-quarter AI orders, revenue and backlog series. Orders vary roughly 20x quarter to quarter, from $1.7B in Q4 FY2025 to $34.1B in Q4 FY2026. The Q3 FY2026 backlog is footnoted to exclude an IREN agreement that moved into Q4 orders, so the series is not a consistent as-of measure. Informs §1, §6 and §13.
  • Storage share by category, on a series later decks stopped publishing. Across the 2023 and 2025 quarterly decks and the analyst-day slide, high-end RAID share was 41% in CY22, 36% in CY25Q2 and 33% in CY25Q4, and external RAID 29% to 24%. The three most recent decks head the slide "Leading Share" and "#1 in all major categories of Storage." Informs §4.
  • The mainstream server share series, restated between two decks seven weeks apart. 2021, 2022 and 2023 were each raised roughly three points and the headline gain moved from about five points to about seven, on a disclosed definitional change adding rack-scale and restricting to x86 non-accelerated. Under either definition the series peaks in 2022 and declines four to five points. Informs §4 and §8.
  • Total revenue per unit of $1,220 against $670 for HP Inc. and Lenovo combined, widening from 1.6x in FY19 Q4, with Dell adding $245 per unit against roughly $45 for the peers. The peer figures are Dell's own calculation from competitors' filings. Informs §1 and §4.
  • Server consolidation ratios and ASP direction. 16G has 2.5–3x cores and 25%–35% greater power efficiency, replacing three to five 14G servers, and 17G has 4–5x cores, replacing five to seven. 17G prices are up 40% over three years on content, and over 70% of the installed base is still on 14G or older. Informs §2 and §6.
  • The physics behind rack-scale content expansion: power per rack rising from roughly 120 kW to 250 kW to 1 MW and GPU density from 72 to 144 to 576 across three generations. Dell sells cold plates, cooling distribution units, manifolds, rear-door heat exchangers, high-voltage DC power distribution, leak detection and telemetry into that shift. Informs §2 and §5.
  • The pre-AI customer-mix baseline: infrastructure to nearly 80% of leading cloud companies with cloud-service-provider customers at roughly 20% of the ISG portfolio as of Q1 FY2022. Informs §1 and §5.
  • The AI customer segmentation and the margin statement inside it: Tier-2 cloud and neocloud, sovereign, and enterprise, with enterprise proof-of-concept work running at margin rates above Tier-2 cloud providers. Management's stated path to a better AI margin is mix shift toward enterprise, not price on the at-scale business. Informs §1 and §3.
  • How far the AI numbers moved in two years. Dell's own 2027 AI hardware-and-services opportunity estimate went from $124B to $310B, projected AI capital expenditure from $200B to $400B-plus, and projected 2028 US data-center power demand from 245TWh to 450TWh, all on the same source family. The 2023 ISG addressable-market series was dropped entirely in 2025 in favour of a cumulative multi-year infrastructure figure. Informs §4 and §6.
  • The core-versus-DFS debt bridge across FY19 to 2Q FY22, which the 10-K presents only as a point estimate: core and other debt $43.3B to $29.0B with core leverage 4.2x to 2.2x, against DFS debt flat to rising. Informs §12.
  • Management naming its own problem on an analyst-day slide: three numbered actions to regain PC momentum and share, the second being to fix consumer and return it to growth. Informs §3 and §10.

Appendix C — External data sources

Two external datasets are available for Dell's businesses. Neither has been pulled.

DRAM and NAND spot and contract pricing (memory_spot_pricing). The dataset is a partial mosaic of dated memory price points drawn from scattered cited sources, because the authoritative TrendForce series is paid. It measures DRAM and NAND contract and spot prices over time. Management names memory as the number-one binding constraint and states that FY2027 revenue is set by supply, and the FY2026 10-K guides to notable component-cost inflation in FY2027. Roughly 61% of the $27B FY2027 guidance raise is in lines the 10-Q attributes primarily to average selling price. The direction and timing of memory prices therefore set both the revenue give-back and the inventory write-down exposure. A dated series would test Section 6's cyclical-versus-secular split and Section 17's traditional-server and CSG price drivers against an observable path, and would give Section 18's first risk a leading indicator with a history. Because it is a mosaic, any figures it produced would be medium-to-low confidence with coverage gaps. Status: not yet pulled (available on demand).

FRED macroeconomic and interest-rate series (fred_series). These are Federal Reserve Economic Data series covering the rate environment, available through a free API. They measure policy and market interest rates over time. Dell Financial Services funds a $14.3B receivable book largely through securitization and structured financing, with $3.0 billion of borrowings exposed to rate fluctuations and 100 basis points worth roughly $30 million of annual interest. Customer financing demand also moves with the rate environment. The series would inform the DFS discussion in Section 12 and, marginally, the financing-enabled demand driver in Section 1. Its reach is limited because Dell's corporate debt is entirely fixed-rate at a 5.24% weighted coupon. Status: not yet pulled (available on demand).
